horoscopes.intro: November 25 in the stars: Find out what’s in store for you today in our daily horoscopes for Wednesday November 25. Read the daily horoscopes for your Sun sign or rising sign (ascendant) to plan your day.

aries.text: Make a point of actually scheduling your holiday fun—otherwise you could work right through it. As your ruling planet, Mars, charges into Virgo and your industrious sixth house for an extra-long visit, until February 21, you’ve got the muscle for your hustle. Before you dive in, put viable systems in place that will keep you on track day in and day out. Everything from fueling yourself with nutritious meals to getting a great night’s sleep will contribute to your productivity. When Mars turns retrograde on January 10, revisit any routines that haven’t stuck rather than piling on new ones. And here’s a pro tip that never gets old, especially for speedy Rams: It’s a marathon, not a sprint!

taurus.text: Your most fetching frocks will be in heavy rotation starting today as firecracker Mars charges into Virgo and your fun-loving fifth house until February 21. Passion and romance fill the air so make the most of this vibe. Attached Bulls could have buzzworthy news to share this season. Single? Attractive prospects could pop up at a holiday party or on the dance floor at a New Year’s Eve bash. Regardless of your relationship status, save some of that magic for a creative project that lights you up. If anything stalls after Mars turns retrograde on January 10, don’t scrap the vision. A few revisions could polish it to a gleam.

gemini.text: Stock up on cocoa, light the fireplace and ready the guest room! Twin Central becomes holiday HQ starting today as activating Mars parades into Virgo and your domestic corner today and hunkers down until February 21. While you love socializing, make sure to leave whitespace on your calendar for alone time, especially once the red planet turns retrograde on January 10. If you don’t, you could get stressed and cranky. You’re geared up to finally tackle a big project around the house, but slow down and create a clear plan of action before you reach for the toolbox.

cancer.text: Say farewell to any fair-weather friends in your midst as proactive Mars barrels into Virgo and your communication sector today. Between now and February 21, fill your free time with stimulating, memorable interactions. Holiday markets, ice-skating dates, ugly-sweater parties…you have places to go and plenty to do! If tantalizing invitations aren’t pouring in, take the bull by the horns and plan the activities YOU want to participate in. You might find an ideal collaborator while you’re at it. Since Mars turns retrograde on January 10, it’s wise to test a creative partnership before making any major commitments.

leo.text: Ever since activating Mars barreled into Leo on September 27, you’ve been on the go—and you might be running on fumes at this point. You’ll have a chance to downshift and get into a slower, steadier groove starting today when the red planet segues into Virgo and your grounded second house until February 21. Press pause and take a moment to get organized. Everything from your calendar to your budget could benefit from a thorough going-over, especially before holiday spending kicks in. You could turn a lucrative idea into a serious moneymaker this winter, so channel your energy into this income-boosting venture. When Mars turns retrograde on January 10, review your numbers before you scale up.

virgo.text: Your mojo returns as mobilizing Mars blasts into your sign today for an extra-long stay, filling you with charisma and motivation until February 21. You’ll wake up on the right side of the bed and hit the ground running for nearly three whole months, so channel this powerful energy into projects that get your blood pumping. Push hardest before January 10, when Mars turns retrograde. At that point, you may need to circle back to a goal or two. Hosting Mars makes you quite the sexy force, but you’re also perfectly happy to enjoy your freedom and play the field. That won’t stop intriguing prospects from chasing after you in hot pursuit. Have fun with it!

libra.text: If you’ve been checking prices of storage units lately, proactive Mars saves the day when it arrives in sensible Virgo and your releasing twelfth house today. Until February 21, you’re motivated to clear your space. Letting go of things you no longer use can give you a rush AND a nice chunk of change. Sell your designer duds online or list those chairs you never use on Facebook Marketplace. And if your closet’s full of skeletons rather than unworn clothes, brave Mars will help you confront them, especially after it turns retrograde on January 10. Look ’em straight in the eye, Libra, and you’ll find they’re not so scary after all.

scorpio.text: Wouldn’t it be nice to celebrate your recent wins with your crew? Ever since your co-ruler, Mars, charged into your achievement camp on September 27, you’ve been on a roll. Starting today, the red planet swings into Virgo and your groups arena until February 21, so get together with friends and see what seasonal fun you can drum up, whether that’s a holiday party or a ski weekend. Just know that feisty Mars can stir up battles that have been simmering with your squad, especially once it turns retrograde on January 10. If it’s time to air grievances, agree on ground rules first so this doesn’t do more harm than good.

sagittarius.text: Aim those arrows sky-high, Archer! With motivational Mars blazing into Virgo and your tenth house of career until February 21, your winning streak starts in 3…2…1. This holiday season may not be as playful as you planned, but the sweat equity you invest while everyone else is in vacation mode will be so worth it. Seek out the movers and shakers at their favorite hangs and make a polished pitch that shows off your inimitable blend of vision and enthusiasm. Try to get it in before January 10, when Mars turns retrograde and decision-makers may stall.

capricorn.text: You won’t be able to stay in one spot for long once adrenalizing Mars bursts into Virgo and your exploratory ninth house today. Until February 21, you’re amped up to break free and pursue exciting new ideas, so don’t plan everything to a T, Capricorn. Go in search of unfamiliar territory, whether that’s a winter getaway or a class that stretches your mind. Since Mars turns retrograde on January 10, build buffer days into any trips and double-check those bookings. The red planet only tours this adventurous part of your chart every two years, so have some fun pushing the envelope!

aquarius.text: Yes or no, Aquarius: What’s it gonna be? You won’t wonder for long, with just-do-it Mars plunging into Virgo and your “all in” eighth house until February 21. You could commit to someone you feel strongly about OR walk away from a casual connection that won’t grow into anything more. Stay open to a soul-deep connection and don’t shy away from intense emotion in your existing relationships. Just be warned: When Mars turns retrograde on January 10, an unresolved issue around shared money or intimacy could come back for a redo.

pisces.text: Dynamic duos, unite! Today, galvanizing Mars barrels into Virgo and activates your seventh house of partnership until February 21. Even the most bashful Fish will find the courage to go after the plus-one you want, whether that’s a business partner or a romantic soulmate. No standing around waiting to be handed a rose! Get right to the point with dates so they know what you’re looking for. Already coupled? This is your once-every-two-years opportunity to tune up your connection or cut bait. And if an ex circles back after Mars turns retrograde on January 10, weigh it carefully before you reopen that door.

items.title: Short-Form Video Use and Adolescent Suicidality, Nonsuicidal Self-Injury, and Mental Health
items.originalTitle: Short-Form Video Use and Adolescent Suicidality, Nonsuicidal Self-Injury, and Mental Health
items.summary: Importance: Short-form video (SFV) use is widespread among adolescents, but measures that capture only viewing time or only addictive use may miss high-risk subgroups.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract:
Importance: Short-form video (SFV) use is widespread among adolescents, but measures that capture only viewing time or only addictive use may miss high-risk subgroups.

Objective: To examine whether SFV viewing time and addictive use are incompletely overlapping and whether transitions and cumulative exposure to a joint high-risk state are associated with suicidal ideation (SI), suicide attempts (SAs), nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI), internalizing problems (IPs), and externalizing problems (EPs).

Design, setting, and participants: This 3-wave prospective cohort study (2022-2024) followed adolescents annually in Southern China. Data were analyzed from November 2025 to April 2026.

Exposures: SFV viewing time and addictive use were jointly classified into 4 use states: low viewing time-low addictive use, high viewing time-low addictive use, low viewing time-high addictive use, and high viewing time-high addictive use.

Main outcomes and measures: At year 3, adolescents reported SI, SAs, and NSSI and completed the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire for IPs and EPs. For each binary outcome at year 3, modified Poisson regression with robust variance was used to estimate adjusted risk ratios (aRRs) and 95% CIs.

Results: The analytic sample included 10 048 adolescents (mean [SD] age at year 1, 13.9 [1.3] years; 5431 female [54.1%]). At year 1, 1025 (10.2%) reported both high viewing time and high addictive use, and 2592 (25.8%) reported either high addictive use or high viewing time. Compared with adolescents who reported neither high addictive use nor high viewing time, changing to the high state on both dimensions was associated with higher risks across all 5 outcomes, whereas remission from the both high state to the neither high state was not associated with significantly higher risks of SI, SAs, or NSSI but remained associated with higher risks of IPs (aRR, 1.63; 95% CI, 1.31-2.04) and EPs (aRR, 2.20; 95% CI, 1.74-2.79). Cumulative exposure to both high addictive use and high viewing time showed graded associations across outcomes. Each additional year of reporting the high state on both dimensions was associated with aRRs of 1.26 (95% CI, 1.20-1.32) for SI, 1.63 (95% CI, 1.47-1.81) for SAs, 1.33 (95% CI, 1.22-1.46) for NSSI, 1.47 (95% CI, 1.39-1.55) for IPs, and 1.66 (95% CI, 1.58-1.76) for EPs.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Generated Content in Manuscripts Submitted to Annals of Neurology
items.originalTitle: Artificial Intelligence-Generated Content in Manuscripts Submitted to Annals of Neurology
items.summary: Since the large language model (LLM) program Chat Generative Pre-trained Transformer (ChatGPT) was introduced in November 2022, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) expanded rapidly in published writing. This has been quantified in many fields, but not in medical journals that focus on neurology and neuroscience.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract:
Objective: Since the large language model (LLM) program Chat Generative Pre-trained Transformer (ChatGPT) was introduced in November 2022, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) expanded rapidly in published writing. This has been quantified in many fields, but not in medical journals that focus on neurology and neuroscience. We sought to characterize the use of LLM in articles submitted before and after ChatGPT became available to the general public, in a neurology journal, Annals of Neurology, that covers all neurology subspecialties.

Methods: The study evaluated manuscripts submitted on movement disorders, dementia, and vascular neurology before and after ChatGPT became available. AI content was measured with LLM-detection platforms Pangram, Originality.ai and GPTZero. Substantial AI was defined as ≥20% of content, or >50% likelihood of AI use. Manuscript type, country of author, country, Human Development Index (HDI), AI disclosure, and publication decision were compared with AI detected.

Results: Of 300 papers submitted after the introduction of ChatGPT, AI was detected by Pangram in 74 (25%) and this was substantial (≥20% of content) in 32 (11%). Substantial AI was more common in brief communications than full research articles (31% vs 10%, p = 0.006) and in vascular neurology articles (17%, vascular; 8%, dementia; and 5%, movement disorders; p = 0.012). Most manuscripts analyzed were submitted by authors from China (37%) and the United States (19%) and each had 11% substantial AI use. Authors from countries with lower levels of development were more likely to use AI (median HDI 0.797, AI ≥20% vs median HDI 0.925, AI <20%, p = 0.033). No AI was found in 60 papers submitted from July 3 to September 14, 2022 (pre-ChatGPT) by any of the AI-detection platforms. Of 300 post-ChatGPT manuscripts, 24 (8%) were accepted. None with substantial AI use were accepted (p = 0.090; odds ratio [OR] = 0.000, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.000-1.068). The authors of 5 (2%) of these papers disclosed AI use, including 1 (3%) of the papers with substantial AI detected.

Interpretation: The study found AI was used in writing one quarter of papers submitted to Annals of Neurology after ChatGPT was introduced, with substantial AI content in 11%. No papers with AI ≥20% of content were accepted for publication. AI-generated text was more frequent in brief communications and vascular neurology articles. items.title: Neuropathologic Correlates of Cognitive Decline in Community-Dwelling Elders Who Die as Centenarians
items.originalTitle: Neuropathologic Correlates of Cognitive Decline in Community-Dwelling Elders Who Die as Centenarians
items.summary: Background and objectives: Brain pathologies are common in the elderly; however, their contribution to Alzheimer dementia risk and cognitive decline in those who die as centenarians remain unclear.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract:
Background and objectives: Brain pathologies are common in the elderly; however, their contribution to Alzheimer dementia risk and cognitive decline in those who die as centenarians remain unclear. This study examines the frequency of Alzheimer disease neuropathologic changes (ADNC), limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy neuropathologic change (LATE-NC), and other brain pathologies and their association with Alzheimer dementia risk and cognitive decline in centenarians.

Methods: This clinicopathologic study included older participants from the Religious Orders Study and Rush Memory and Aging Project, 2 ongoing clinicopathologic cohort studies of aging and dementia, who underwent annual clinical evaluations and autopsy. Participants were evaluated annually for cognitive status and followed for a mean (SD) of 11.4 (5.3) years before death. Neuropathologic evaluation included ADNC (and separately β-amyloid load and tangle density), LATE-NC, presence or absence of neocortical Lewy bodies (LBs), hippocampal sclerosis of aging (HS-A), primary age-related tauopathy (PART), and 5 cerebrovascular disease (CVD) pathologies including arteriolosclerosis, atherosclerosis, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, macroinfarcts, and microinfarcts. Multivariable regression and linear mixed-effects models were applied.

Results: A total of 104 centenarians were included in this study. The mean (SD) age at death was 102 (1.9) years, 84% were female, 58% had Alzheimer dementia, 21% had mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and 21% had no cognitive impairment (NCI). All 3 clinical diagnostic groups exhibited pathologies, including any type of CVD (94%), ADNC (72%; 73% of them were intermediate and 27% of them were high), LATE-NC (58%, 30% of them exhibiting HS-A), HS-A (18%, 95% had LATE-NC), PART (28%), and neocortical LBs (11%). Mixed pathologies, particularly ADNC + LATE-NC + CVD, were common in the Alzheimer dementia group (52%) compared with NCI (36%) and MCI (23%). After adjusted for age at death, sex, education, and other brain pathologies, only LATE-NC and tangles (specifically intermediate/high ADNC with Braak stage V) were associated with more rapid decline in global cognition and increased odds of Alzheimer dementia.

Discussion: Brain pathology, but not dementia, is nearly inevitable in those who die as centenarians. LATE-NC and tangles are the key contributors to cognitive decline. Future study investigating resilience factors may inform preventive strategies.

items.title: A shared meaning component across languages in the human brain
items.originalTitle: A shared meaning component across languages in the human brain
items.summary: Human languages differ profoundly in their sounds, words and grammatical systems, yet all support the communication of complex meanings. How the brain handles this diversity remains a fundamental question in language neuroscience.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Human languages differ profoundly in their sounds, words and grammatical systems, yet all support the communication of complex meanings. How the brain handles this diversity remains a fundamental question in language neuroscience. Multilingual neural network models offer a way to answer this question by representing linguistic content across languages in a shared space. Leveraging these advances, we evaluated the similarity of linguistic representations in speakers of 21 languages. Here we combined existing (12 languages across 4 language families) and newly collected functional magnetic resonance imaging data (9 languages across 4 families) to test encoding models predicting brain activity in the language network using representations from multilingual models. Model representations predicted brain responses reliably within each language. Critically, encoding models trained on one set of languages generalized zero-shot to previously unseen languages, accurately predicting neural responses without exposure to the target language. This cross-lingual generalization extended across variation in language family, stimulus type and presentation modality. These findings point to a shared cross-lingual component for meaning across human languages.

items.title: Phase coding supports neuronal replication and enables combinatorial problem solving
items.originalTitle: Phase coding supports neuronal replication and enables combinatorial problem solving
items.summary: Darwinian neurodynamics posits that the brain searches large solution spaces through iterated cycles of variation and selection on competing neural representations.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
items.abstract: Darwinian neurodynamics posits that the brain searches large solution spaces through iterated cycles of variation and selection on competing neural representations. Testing this hypothesis requires a biologically plausible neural replicator: a mechanism that copies spatiotemporal signals faithfully enough to cumulatively improve good solutions, yet loosely enough to allow exploration. We show that phase-coded spike patterns constitute such a replicator. Spike timing referenced to a local field oscillation is compressed into a transferable spike train and reconstructed by coincidence with the receiver's own field, without synaptic plasticity or a shared code key. As replication noise rises, the system crosses two thresholds. Below the first, faithful copying sustains patterns as dynamic memory. Between the two thresholds, pattern populations evolve. On two hard combinatorial benchmarks, the traveling salesman problem and NK fitness landscapes, neural replication remains competitive with standard search methods at a matched evaluation budget. Beyond the second, an Eigen-like error threshold, inherited information collapses. The network architecture tunes the exploration-exploitation balance: high-degree lattices, where local competition is stronger, exploit smooth landscapes, while low-degree lattices, where weaker competition preserves diversity, search more broadly on rugged landscapes. The framework predicts phase-locked information transfer and phylogenetic structure in replay, as well as a selective loss of combinatorial problem solving beyond the error threshold. These results indicate that a single neurobiological substrate can support memory, variation, and selection, and point to evolutionary dynamics as a candidate computational principle for cognition.

items.title: High-performance annealing-free wurtzite ferroelectric field-effect transistors with ultrathin oxide semiconductors for neuromorphic computing
items.originalTitle: High-performance annealing-free wurtzite ferroelectric field-effect transistors with ultrathin oxide semiconductors for neuromorphic computing
items.summary: Wurtzite-structured aluminum scandium nitride (AlScN) ferroelectric materials are potential candidates for non-volatile memory (NVM) applications because of their high remanent polarization (Pr > 100 μC·cm-2) and compatibility with back-end-of-line (BEOL) processes.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Wurtzite-structured aluminum scandium nitride (AlScN) ferroelectric materials are potential candidates for non-volatile memory (NVM) applications because of their high remanent polarization (Pr > 100 μC·cm-2) and compatibility with back-end-of-line (BEOL) processes. However, achieving high-performance wurtzite ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs) remains a significant challenge because of their high interface trap density (Dit) and large threshold voltage (VTH) variation. Here we show the distinct polarization switching mechanisms of AlScN FeFETs based on an ultrathin indium gallium oxide (IGO) channel with three different structures. FeFETs with a metal-ferroelectric-metal-insulator-semiconductor (MFMIS) structure show high interface quality with low Dit and a stable VTH, achieving a large memory window (MW) of up to 20.6 V and a high endurance of 106. The stable 6-bit operation of our devices with 64 distinct states shows the feasibility of multilevel storage applications. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of the FeFET in neuromorphic networks, with a high recognition accuracy of 93.02%.

items.title: Nitric oxide feedback to ciliary photoreceptor cells gates a UV avoidance circuit
items.originalTitle: Nitric oxide feedback to ciliary photoreceptor cells gates a UV avoidance circuit
items.summary: Nitric oxide (NO) produced by nitric oxide synthase (NOS) is a key regulator of animal physiology. Here, we uncover a function for NO in the integration of UV exposure and the gating of a UV-avoidance circuit.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Nitric oxide (NO) produced by nitric oxide synthase (NOS) is a key regulator of animal physiology. Here, we uncover a function for NO in the integration of UV exposure and the gating of a UV-avoidance circuit. We studied UV/violet avoidance mediated by brain ciliary photoreceptors (cPRCs) in larvae of the annelid Platynereis dumerilii. In the larva, NOS is expressed in interneurons (INNOS) postsynaptic to cPRCs. UV stimulation of cPRCs triggers INNOS activation and NO production. NO signals retrogradely to cPRCs to induce their sustained post-stimulus activation through an unconventional guanylate cyclase. This late activation drives ciliary beating through serotonergic ciliomotor neurons during UV avoidance. In NOS mutants, retrograde signalling, ciliary activation, and UV avoidance are defective. By mathematical modelling, we recapitulate phototransduction and circuit dynamics in wild-type and mutant larvae. Our results reveal how NO-mediated retrograde signalling gates a synaptic circuit and induces short-term memory of UV exposure to orchestrate light-avoidance behaviour.

items.abstract: Educational attainment and mental health are associated from childhood, but less is known about how this association is reflected within families, where children's genetic variation is correlated with both parental genotypes and family environments. We examine whether associations involving children's own and parental polygenic scores differ for cognitive and non-cognitive genetic components of educational attainment. These scores aggregate common DNA variants using weights from genome-wide association studies. We analyse 3,223 mother-father-child trios from the UK Millennium Cohort Study using structural equation models that jointly estimate associations involving children's own and parental polygenic scores. Here we show that cognitive and non-cognitive education-related polygenic scores are associated with externalising behaviour, including hyperactivity and conduct problems, and internalising behaviour, including anxiety and low mood, across childhood and adolescence. Associations are generally larger in magnitude for externalising than internalising behaviour, with clearer component-specific differences for externalising behaviour. These findings highlight the heterogeneity in education-related polygenic score associations with youth mental health within families.

items.title: Neural subspaces encode sequential working memory without detectable neural sequences
items.originalTitle: Neural subspaces encode sequential working memory without detectable neural sequences
items.summary: The neural mechanisms of multiple-item working memory are not well understood. In the current study, we address two competing hypotheses about the neural basis of sequential working memory: neural subspaces versus neural sequences.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: The neural mechanisms of multiple-item working memory are not well understood. In the current study, we address two competing hypotheses about the neural basis of sequential working memory: neural subspaces versus neural sequences. Using broadband MEG data from human participants, we applied dimensionality reduction and multivariate decoding techniques to test whether a sequence of items is maintained through the reactivation of individual items in sequence (neural sequences) or by organizing them into distinct low-dimensional subspaces (neural subspaces). Our results revealed behaviorally relevant, low-dimensional neural subspaces that organized memory representations according to ordinal position in the sequence, supporting the neural subspaces hypothesis. In contrast, we found no evidence of sequential neural replay during the retention period, contrary to the neural sequences hypothesis. In this work, we show that sequential working memory is maintained through structured geometric organization in low-dimensional representational space, rather than through the sequential reactivation of individual items, thus clarifying the mechanisms of multi-item working memory.

items.title: Neural correlates of facial recognition in a social wasp
items.originalTitle: Neural correlates of facial recognition in a social wasp
items.summary: In humans and other primates, faces are special visual objects that are encoded by circuits selective to faces.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: In humans and other primates, faces are special visual objects that are encoded by circuits selective to faces. If specialized circuits are the most efficient way to encode and discriminate among similar-looking objects of high relevance, then we expect that analogous circuits should evolve in other taxa with specialized visual individual recognition abilities. Thus, we surveyed the neural responses to visual objects across the brain of a wasp that has independently evolved specialized facial recognition, Polistes fuscatus. We found a localized population of neurons analogous to face cells, which we term "wasp cells," that selectively fire to front-facing wasp images. Some of these wasp cells encode information about facial patterns, which possibly underlie the unique visual recognition abilities of these wasps. These findings demonstrate high-level feature-selective tuning in an invertebrate and suggest that specialized circuits are an adaptive feature for nervous systems requiring complex visual recognition.
